question: In August 2026, the Commission presented a proposal for Baltic fishing quotas in 2027. It provides for cuts in the bycatch limits for cod of 88% and 51% and an increase in the limits for sprat of 44%. In light of the above: 1.

Why does the Commission consider it proportionate and reasonable to further mechanically tighten restrictions on the fishing sector, given that the bans in force since 2019 have not led to the recovery of cod stocks and that factors not linked to fishing are having a significant impact on the situation?

When proposing to increase the catch limit for sprat by 44%, how did the Commission take into account the requirement to apply an ecosystem-based approach and the key importance of this species in the diet of cod?

How has the Commission assessed the risk that setting bycatch limits on the basis of the bycatch reported in 2025, in the absence of a level set by ICES, will lead to the premature closure of mixed fisheries and drastically impact the coastal fleet?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.10.2026) For several years the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) has advised to stop all catches of cod. To avoid choking fisheries which by-catch cod, total allowable catches (TAC) are set, but limited to by-catches only. The TAC should however not exceed actual needs because as few cod as possible should be fished.

The Commission proposal is based on the latest available data, i.e. the reported landings of cod per Member State in 2025. As regards sprat, the Commission proposal is based on the latest scientific advice from ICES which estimates that the sprat biomass has almost doubled and is expected to increase further, and that the TAC can be increased by 44%.

The proposed TACs are 211 tonnes of eastern cod and 31 tonnes of western cod. Member States can swap quotas. Total annual EU landings reported by the Member States to the Commission were 110-202 tonnes (since 2021) of eastern cod, and 42 tonnes (2024) and 19 tonnes (2025) of western cod. By the end of September 2026 total reported EU landings in 2026 were 32 tonnes and 7 tonnes, respectively.
